growth_story.headline: Sudan's income per person peaked in 2011, slid after the oil went with South Sudan, then collapsed in the war that began in 2023.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2007 income per person grew 3.0 percent a year, and the World Bank describes 2000 to 2010 as the oil boom years. In 2008 to 2017 growth fell to -0.8 percent a year. Income per person peaked in 2011, the year South Sudan seceded and took most of the oil, its exports and much of the state's revenue. From 2018 to 2025 it fell 8.7 percent a year: first through political turmoil, very high inflation and a short-lived recovery cut off by COVID and the 2021 military takeover, then through the war that began in April 2023. Income per person fell 30.4 percent in 2023 and 14.7 percent in 2024, then grew just 0.6 percent in 2025. It is now 58.1 percent below its 2011 peak and lower than in 1960, the first year of the record.

threads.title: Oil boom, then secession
threads.text: The World Bank calls 2000 to 2010 Sudan's oil boom years. When South Sudan seceded in 2011, most oil fields went with it, and Sudan lost most of its oil production, exports and state revenue. Growth never regained its earlier pace.

threads.title: Debt, sanctions and isolation
threads.text: In the years after secession, Sudan carried debts in arrears, faced US sanctions and lost links to foreign banks. This limited its access to outside finance.

citations.title: Sudan: 2017 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 17/364)
citations.quote: arrears and limited access to external financing, U.S. sanctions, and the withdrawal of correspondent bank relations

threads.title: Inflation and a derailed recovery
threads.text: From 2018 the economy shrank amid political upheaval and very high inflation, as the budget was financed by printing money. Reforms brought a brief recovery, but COVID and the 2021 military takeover ended it and halted debt relief and foreign aid.

citations.title: Sudan: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2024
citations.quote: Economic activity continued to decline over the period 2018-22, affected by growing political instability, hyperinflation amid currency pressures, and fiscal deficit monetization.

citations.title: Sudan: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2024
citations.quote: the 2021 military intervention that halted debt relief efforts under HIPC and suspended foreign assistance inflows

threads.title: War since April 2023
threads.text: The war that began in April 2023 caused a severe economic contraction. Damage to services, mostly in Khartoum, was a major driver, and the economy shrank sharply for two years in a row.

citations.title: Sudan: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026
citations.quote: The conflict that erupted in April 2023 has caused severe economic contraction and reversed development gains.

citations.title: Sudan: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2024
citations.quote: a major driver is the damage to the services sector (medical, educational, telecommunications, retail and wholesale services), which is mostly concentrated in Khartoum

citations.title: Sudan: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2024
citations.quote: The economy is expected to shrink to two-thirds of its pre-conflict size after a second year of double-digit contraction

threads.title: A fragile, gold-led rebound
threads.text: Where security improved, production and trade picked up and growth resumed in 2025, with gold the main export. The recovery starts from a very low base and depends on how the conflict unfolds.

citations.title: Sudan: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026

since_last_year.text: A modest recovery took hold in 2025 as security improved in some regions. In 2026 inflation picked up again and the pound fell sharply, as the conflict in the Middle East raised fuel and import costs. The emergence of a rival authority has added to the risks.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes a rebound in 2025, but in the data income per person grew only 0.6 percent that year, so little of the recovery shows up per person, most likely because the population kept growing. The same goes for the mid-2010s: the IMF reported GDP growth in 2016, while income per person grew 0.4 percent. The World Bank's own estimate of how far the economy fell in 2023 was also revised sharply between editions.
